reconcile.note: Gill treats the Raamah-line Dedan of Genesis 10 and the Jokshan-line Dedan of Genesis 25 as two distinct Arabian peoples who happen to share a recurring tribal name.

discrepancy.note: Colenso reads the double placement of Dedan among both Ham's and Abraham's descendants as a genuine discrepancy in the text's genealogical tradition.

quotes.text: But there are several discrepancies in this account, which show some uncertainty in the traditions, reports, or theories, on which the writer relies; and there are other points, on which it is at variance with the ethnological science of the present day.
quotes.attr: John William Colenso (d. 1883), The Pentateuch and Book of Joshua Critically Examined, Vol. IV (1863), critical analysis of Genesis, on Genesis 10:7 and 25:3.

quotes.text: But if so, then both Sheba and Dedan, who are reckoned together as grandsons of the Shemite, Abraham, xxv.3, must be connected with the Hamite Sheba and Dedan of x.7.
quotes.attr: John William Colenso (d. 1883), The Pentateuch and Book of Joshua Critically Examined, Vol. IV (1863), critical analysis of Genesis, on Genesis 10:7 and 25:3.

sides.snippet: The sons of Raamah: Sheba and Dedan.
sides.verseText: The sons of Cush: Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah, and Sabteca. The sons of Raamah: Sheba and Dedan.

sides.snippet: Jokshan became the father of Sheba, and Dedan.
sides.verseText: Jokshan became the father of Sheba, and Dedan. The sons of Dedan were Asshurim, Letushim, and Leummim.
